parts.name: The cathedral
parts.stand: In Mitropoleos Square, facing the cathedral's front.

paras.t: This is the Metropolitan Cathedral of the Annunciation, the cathedral of the Archbishop of Athens and all Greece. King Otto and Queen Amalia laid its first stone on Christmas Day 1842.
It wasn't quick. It took several architects and 20 years, and builders used marble from 72 demolished churches. It was dedicated in May 1862.

Inside lie two people Greeks hold very dear. Saint Philothei, martyred in 1589, remembered for buying the freedom of Greek women enslaved under Ottoman rule. And Patriarch Gregory the Fifth, hanged in 1821 in revenge for the Greek uprising. Greek sailors rescued his body, and eventually it was enshrined here in Athens.
If a service is on, step in quietly. A good rule of thumb for Greek churches: no short sleeves or bare legs, as a mark of respect.

parts.name: The Little Metropolis
parts.stand: Walk to the small stone church just south of the cathedral.

paras.t: Now look at this little church beside the giant. It's Saint Eleftherios, nicknamed the Little Metropolis.
We don't yet have a source we trust for its history, so we won't guess. It's well worth a slow walk around the outside.
In the square, the two statues are Constantine the Eleventh, the last Byzantine emperor, and Archbishop Damaskinos, who led the church in Athens through the Second World War.
